method: waitpid reports a child in one 16-bit integer: the exit code occupies bits 8 to 15, the terminating signal the low seven bits, and bit 7 is the core-dump flag, which is why a SIGSEGV with a core is 0x008b and a plain exit(1) is 0x0100. WIFEXITED is true when the low seven bits are zero, WEXITSTATUS is status >> 8 & 0xff, and otherwise WIFSIGNALED is true unless the low seven bits are 0x7f, which marks a stopped child with WSTOPSIG in the high byte; 0xffff is the one status WIFCONTINUED reports. Shells collapse this to eight bits: a process that exits reports its code unchanged, while a process killed by signal n appears as 128 + n, so 130 is SIGINT, 137 SIGKILL, 139 SIGSEGV and 143 SIGTERM. bash reports 127 when a command is not found and 126 when it is found but cannot be executed, and it truncates exit codes modulo 256, so exit(-1) arrives as 255. The 128 + n range covers 129 to 192 for the 64 Linux signals (129 to 159 for the named signals 1 to 31, 160 to 192 for the real-time range, with 32 and 33 reserved by the C library), while 128 itself and 193 to 255 are ordinary exit codes. Because the shell keeps only those eight bits, a program that calls exit(139) is indistinguishable from a SIGSEGV death and the core flag is lost, so the shell mode marks the core state as not visible and the raw wait status as not recoverable. Values are decimal or 0x hexadecimal, from 0 to 255 in shell mode and 0 to 65535 in raw mode; a status that encodes a stop signal of 0 or above 64, or a terminating signal above 64, is refused because the kernel never writes it. The reference table lists signals 1 to 31 with their default actions from signal(7). Everything is integer arithmetic in the browser: nothing is executed, stored or sent anywhere.
